newsitem.title: UK: Sierra Leone coup may demand military force - UK, UN.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coup may demand military force - UK, UN.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said on Wednesday that a military solution might have to be considered as a last resort to reinstate civilian rule in strife-torn Sierra Leone.

Annan and Cook told reporters after an hour-long meeting they both preferred a peaceful end to the stand-off between junior officers who led a coup on May 25 and Nigerian forces trying to restore democracy in the west African country.

"Ideally, I would prefer negotiations... It must be clear to the coup leaders that they don't have the support of the people, they don't have the support of their neighbours, they don't have the support of the region and they don't have the support of the international community," Annan said.

"How they expect to survive I do not know. I wish they would be sensible and cut their losses and walk away," he said, adding he was hopeful that international pressure would make the coup leaders see the "senselessness of their enterprise".
Pressed to say whether he would back military intervention, Annan said: "I maintain what I've said -- that if use of force becomes a last resort and is inevitable, it may have to come to that."

Annan stopped over in London on his return from an Organisation of African Unity summit in Zimbabwe, where some delegates said African leaders resolved to isolate the rebel government and back west African efforts to restore democracy.
But at least one West African leader expressed reservations about a military solution to the conflict.
"The agreements between the states of West Africa do not authorise military intervention to restore a regime or organise a counter-coup," Burkina Faso's Blaise Compaore said in Harare.
Cook, whose government had previously shied away from endorsing the use of force to overturn the coup, agreed with Annan that it might become inevitable.
"At the present time we would much rather see a resolution of this by negotiation...

"Ultimately military force may be something that will have to be considered, but at the present time if these people have any common sense they would recognise that they are not going to assist themselves by trying to stay on by force and they are only going to damage other parts of the country," Cook said.
